passage:
"Give me the remote, baby!" Tejas shouted, and shoved his little brother off the sofa.
Suraj landed on the floor. He felt tiny. "I was watching first," he whispered.
"Get lost!"
Suraj ran to the kitchen. "Mummy, Tejas pushed me. My elbow hurts."
Mummy turned off the stove and came straight in. "Tejas, stop. No pushing. Suraj, let me see your elbow." She rubbed it. "Now I want to hear both of you. Suraj first, then Tejas."
Suraj sniffed. "It's not fair."
"You did the right thing telling me," Mummy said.

qa.q: What did Mummy turn off before she came in?
qa.a: Mummy turned off the stove and came straight in.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after he landed on the floor?
qa.a: He felt tiny and helpless, hurt in his elbow and in his feelings, and unsure he could stand up to his big brother.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that a wise parent would do?
qa.a: She stopped the pushing at once, checked Suraj's elbow and asked to hear both boys before deciding anything.

qa.q: How might Tejas see Mummy's decision to hear both sides?
qa.a: He may feel caught but also relieved that he gets a turn to explain, instead of just being shouted at.

grounding: A younger child is shouted at and pushed by his older brother, tells a parent, and the parent stops the hurting and listens to both.

passage:
Note for the boys' mother, from their after-school carer.
At the building swings today, Tarun wanted Suraj's turn. He shouted, "Move, stupid!" and pushed Suraj off. Suraj sat on the ground very small and still, holding his knee. He did not cry at first, then came to me and said, "Tarun hurt me." I told Tarun, "Stop. Pushing is not okay," and checked Suraj's knee (a small scrape, cleaned). Then I sat with both boys and heard each one. Tarun said he was cross about losing at school. Suraj said he felt too small to push back. Both are calmer now.

qa.q: What did Tarun shout before pushing Suraj?
qa.a: He shouted, "Move, stupid!"

qa.q: What does Suraj sitting very small and still suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt helpless and frightened, as if he were too small to push back against his brother.

qa.q: What did the carer do after Suraj said Tarun hurt him?
qa.a: The carer stopped the pushing, cleaned the scrape and then listened to both boys before deciding what to do.

qa.q: How might the boys' mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She may feel sad that Suraj was hurt but reassured that the carer stepped in and listened to both sons.

grounding: A younger boy is pushed by his older brother, tells an adult, and the adult stops it and listens to both sides.

passage: At the gym class, Papa sat on the bench and waved. Vikas and Manoj both ran for the rope. "Me first!" Vikas reached it, looked back at Papa and puffed his chest. Manoj stopped still. His face crumpled. He did not try the balance beam after that. The coach came over. "Manoj, you ran really fast. And I saw you try the beam last week, all by yourself." Later, Papa said, "Vikas, tomorrow you and I will do puzzles. Manoj, you and I will go to the library. Your own special times." Manoj looked up.

qa.q: What did Vikas reach first?
qa.a: Vikas reached the rope first.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling when his face crumpled?
qa.a: He felt crushed and left behind after losing the race, and too discouraged to try the balance beam.

qa.q: What did the coach and Papa do well?
qa.a: The coach praised Manoj's effort, and Papa gave each boy his own special time, so being first mattered less.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when Papa plans separate special times?
qa.a: He may feel pleased to have Papa to himself and less need to beat his brother to be noticed.

grounding: Two brothers race to be first for their father's attention, and a coach and parent praise effort and give each child special time.

passage:
Monday: "I'm first to finish my milk, Papa!" Payal shouted. Naveen slammed his cup down, still half full, and cried.
Wednesday: Naveen raced Payal up the stairs and won. He jumped about. Payal sat on the top step and sulked.
Saturday: Papa set out two sheets of paper. "No race today. I want to see how carefully you each draw our house." Payal coloured slowly. Naveen added a cat. Papa looked at both. "Payal, you tried the windows three times. Naveen, look at that careful tail." Nobody asked who was first.

qa.q: What did Naveen add to his drawing on Saturday?
qa.a: Naveen added a cat to his drawing.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel on Wednesday after winning the stairs race?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited, jumping about, while Payal felt crushed.

qa.q: What did Papa change on Saturday, and why did it help?
qa.a: He set a task with no race and praised each child's effort, so neither had to win to be noticed.

qa.q: How might Payal feel when Papa praises her windows?
qa.a: She probably feels seen and proud of her careful work, without needing to beat Naveen. 😊

grounding: Over a week, a sister and brother race for their father's attention, and he shifts to praising each child's effort instead of who is first.

passage:
Monday: Vaibhav and Parveen both grabbed the blue block and both cried. Mummy said, "Vaibhav, say sorry." He mumbled "Sorry" to the floor. Parveen kept crying. Vaibhav still felt heavy inside.
Tuesday: Vaibhav watched Parveen building alone. He fetched his red fire truck, the one he never lent. He held it out. "Sorry I snatched. You can have the truck." Parveen's face opened like a flower. Vaibhav felt light, like a balloon.
Thursday: They built a fire station together, and the truck lived in it.

qa.q: Which toy did Vaibhav hold out to Parveen?
qa.a: He held out his red fire truck, the one he never lent.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel after his real apology on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt light and happy, like a balloon, instead of heavy inside.

qa.q: Why did Tuesday's sorry work better than Monday's?
qa.a: On Monday he was told to say sorry and mumbled it to the floor; on Tuesday he chose to say sorry and did something kind, so it felt real to both.

qa.q: How might Parveen see the fire truck?
qa.a: She likely feels surprised and happy, seeing that her brother really means sorry because he shared his special toy.

grounding: Over a few days, a child moves from a forced, empty sorry to a real apology with a kind act, and feels light again.

passage: The train was crowded and hot, and the fan above their seat wasn't working. Vaibhav and his sister Salma had fought over the window seat until both were crying. Ammi had no space to separate them. Vaibhav wiped his face and looked at Salma, who was still hiccuping. He dug in his bag and found his little plastic horse. "Here. Sorry I pushed you," he said. "You can have the window for two stations." Salma took the horse and squeezed his hand. Vaibhav felt his tummy go light.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav find in his bag?
qa.a: He found his little plastic horse.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel after he said sorry and gave the horse?
qa.a: He felt relieved and light, his tummy no longer tight from the fight.

qa.q: What makes Vaibhav's apology a good repair?
qa.a: He chose to say sorry for pushing and backed it with kind actions, the horse and a turn at the window.

qa.q: What is it like for Salma when Vaibhav hands her the horse?
qa.a: She feels comforted and cared for, and squeezes his hand to show the fight is over. 🤍

grounding: On a crowded train, after a fight where both siblings cried, a boy says sorry and shares a toy, and feels light again.

passage:
"Anand, why are you standing by the slide alone?" Gurpreet called.
"That big boy took my ball and said I'm a baby."
Gurpreet stopped. That morning, she and Anand had fought over the last paratha. She walked over and stood right beside him.
"Give it back," she said to the big boy. "He's my brother."
"Make me."
Gurpreet's hands curled up. Then she took Anand's hand instead. "Come on. We're telling Miss Das."
"Miss Das, that boy took my brother's ball."
Miss Das went straight over. Anand held his sister's hand the whole time.

qa.q: What had Gurpreet and Anand fought over that morning?
qa.a: They had fought over the last paratha.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet's hands curl up?
qa.a: She felt angry and protective when the big boy said "Make me," and part of her wanted to fight.

qa.q: Which choice of Gurpreet's was wise?
qa.a: She took Anand's hand and told Miss Das instead of fighting the bigger boy.

qa.q: How might Anand feel with his sister beside him?
qa.a: He probably feels safe and less alone, and surprised she helped after their fight.

grounding: A girl stands by her little brother when an older child bothers him, despite their fight at home, and tells a teacher instead of fighting.

passage:
Note for the parents of Dolma and Ojas, from their class teacher.
Dolma and Ojas arrived today not speaking to each other; Dolma told me they fought about a colouring book. At break, two children laughed at Ojas for falling in the sandpit. Dolma saw it, walked across the whole playground and stood next to him. She did not shout. She held his hand and came to find me. "They're laughing at my brother." I spoke to the other children. Dolma and Ojas shared biscuits afterwards. 🙂

qa.q: What had Dolma and Ojas fought about?
qa.a: Dolma told the teacher they fought about a colouring book.

qa.q: What does Dolma walking across the playground to Ojas suggest?
qa.a: She felt protective and loving toward her brother; her care for him was stronger than her anger from the fight.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that shows wise loyalty?
qa.a: She stood beside Ojas, did not shout or fight, and came to tell the teacher.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel when his sister takes his hand?
qa.a: He may feel comforted and surprised, knowing she is on his side even after their argument.

grounding: A young girl stands beside her brother when others laugh at him, though they had fought, and tells the teacher instead of fighting.

passage:
"Mummy, Trisha scribbled on my notebook!"
"And you pushed her. Reena, you are older, you should know better."
"But she did it first!"
"You're older. Say sorry."
Reena stomped into her room and hid under the blanket. "Nobody listens to me," she muttered.
That night, Papa knocked. "I heard there was a fight. Tell me what happened. Then I'll ask Trisha too."
Reena peeped out. "She scribbled on my homework page. Then I pushed."
"Pushing isn't okay. And scribbling isn't either. You'll both say sorry tomorrow."
Reena came out from the blanket.

qa.q: What did Trisha scribble on?
qa.a: She scribbled on Reena's notebook, on her homework page.

qa.q: Why did Reena hide under the blanket?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and hurt that only she was blamed, so she sulked and felt that nobody listened to her.

qa.q: What did Papa do differently from Mummy?
qa.a: He heard both children before deciding, and named what each one did wrong.

qa.q: How might Trisha see being blamed along with Reena?
qa.a: She may feel a bit caught, but it teaches her that scribbling on her sister's work matters too.

grounding: An older child is blamed just for being older and sulks at the unfairness; the other parent hears both sides before deciding.

passage:
From Kishore's notebook, after tonight's fight between my two sons.
Thomas and his little brother were fighting over the tablet. I heard a crash and shouted, "Thomas, you are older, you should know better!" Thomas went red, threw himself on his bed and would not look at me. At dinner he pushed his rice around. Later I asked both boys to tell me, one at a time. The little one admitted he grabbed the tablet and dropped it. Thomas had only shouted. I told Thomas I was sorry. Next time I will ask before I decide.

qa.q: What were Thomas and his little brother fighting over?
qa.a: They were fighting over the tablet.

qa.q: How was Thomas feeling when he threw himself on the bed?
qa.a: He felt blamed unfairly and resentful, so he sulked and would not look at Kishore.

qa.q: What will Kishore do differently next time?
qa.a: Kishore will ask both boys what happened before deciding who is to blame.

qa.q: What is it like for the little brother when both boys are asked to tell their side?
qa.a: He may feel a little guilty for letting Thomas take the blame, but also relieved to own up about the dropped tablet.

grounding: An adult blames the older boy for being older, sees him sulk, then hears both children and apologises.

passage:
"Sarika, why are you so quiet?" Mummy asked at the school gate.
"There's a girl next to me. Vasudha. She has a yellow hairband."
"Do you like her?"
"Yes. But my heart goes boom-boom."
Next morning, Sarika sat down and held her crayon tight. "Vasudha, do you want to play at break?"
Vasudha looked up. "Yes! Can we play house?"
At pick-up, Sarika ran to Mummy. "I asked! She said yes! We played house, and I was the granny!"
Mummy laughed. "That was brave, beti."

qa.q: What colour was Vasudha's hairband?
qa.a: Vasudha's hairband was yellow.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel before she asked Vasudha to play?
qa.a: She felt nervous and shy, her heart going boom-boom, even though she liked Vasudha.

qa.q: What small step helped Sarika start a friendship?
qa.a: She asked a simple, kind question, "Do you want to play at break?", even though she was nervous. 🙂

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Sarika asks her to play?
qa.a: Vasudha probably feels happy and wanted, since she says yes straight away and suggests a game.

grounding: A shy young girl gathers courage to ask the girl next to her to play, and feels brave and happy when she says yes.

passage:
Class notes, from the Butterfly room teacher.
Pallavi has been watching Harsha for days. Harsha is a new girl who sits next to her at the craft table. Today I saw Pallavi hold her own hands tight and take a big breath. Then she leaned over and whispered, "Do you want to play with me?" Harsha nodded and smiled. They spent all of free time at the dough table making snakes. At home time Pallavi told me, "My heart was jumping but I did it." I told her that was a brave start. 😊

qa.q: Where did Pallavi and Harsha spend free time?
qa.a: They spent all of free time at the dough table making snakes.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she held her hands tight?
qa.a: She felt nervous, her heart jumping, but she also liked Harsha and wanted to be friends.

qa.q: How could the teacher help this new friendship grow?
qa.a: The teacher can seat them together and praise Pallavi's brave first move, as the note shows.

qa.q: How might Harsha, the new girl, see Pallavi's whisper?
qa.a: She may feel welcomed and relieved to have a friend in a new class.

grounding: A shy child makes the first move to befriend the new girl beside her, and feels brave when she says yes.

passage: The children in the colony were playing catch near the water tank. Samir stood by the gate, holding the bars and watching. Nobody looked at him. He waited and waited. His mother, Yamini, came out with the rubbish bag and saw him. She crouched beside him. "Want to try the magic words? 'Can I play too?'" Samir shook his head. "Let's practise. I'll be the big kids." Samir whispered it. Then said it louder. Yamini walked with him halfway. Samir took three more steps alone. "Can I play too?" A boy threw him the ball.

qa.q: Where were the children playing catch?
qa.a: They were playing catch near the water tank in the colony.

qa.q: What does Samir holding the gate bars suggest?
qa.a: He felt shy and nervous; he wanted to join but hoped someone would notice him first.

qa.q: What did Yamini do that helped Samir's shyness?
qa.a: She practised the words with him, walked halfway and let him take the last steps alone.

qa.q: How might the boy who threw the ball see Samir?
qa.a: He may simply see a new player and feel happy to have one more person in the game.

grounding: A shy boy waits at the edge of a game, and his mother helps him practise asking to join.

passage:
"Rajni, why are you standing by the tree? The girls are skipping."
"I'm waiting, Mumma."
"Waiting for what?"
"For them to say come."
Sharmila sat on the bench. "What if you ask? Let's practise. I'm a skipping girl. Go."
"Can I... play too?"
"Louder, like you mean it."
"Can I play too?"
"Good! Being shy is okay. It gets smaller every time you try."
Rajni walked to the rope. Her voice was small but clear. "Can I play too?"
"Yes! You hold one end!"

qa.q: What were the girls doing?
qa.a: The girls were skipping.

qa.q: Why was Rajni standing by the tree?
qa.a: She felt shy and unsure, and she was waiting for the girls to invite her instead of asking.

qa.q: What did Sharmila say about shyness that could help Rajni?
qa.a: She said being shy is okay and gets smaller every time you try, and she let Rajni practise first.

qa.q: How might the skipping girls feel when Rajni asks?
qa.a: They seem pleased to include her, and happily give her a job holding the rope.

grounding: A shy girl waits at the edge of a game, and her mother helps her practise asking to join.

passage:
Diary note from Ganga's teacher.
Ganga came in quiet today; she had a cold and was late. Gargi had saved her a seat on the story mat by putting her own water bottle on it. When Ganga sat down, Gargi said, "You're my best friend." Ganga smiled all through story time. At lunch Ganga saved Gargi the last orange slice. Gargi whispered a secret about a surprise card for her mum, and Ganga kept it, only giggling. They are learning to choose each other.

qa.q: How did Gargi save a seat for Ganga?
qa.a: Gargi put her own water bottle on the story mat.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when Gargi called her best friend?
qa.a: She felt special and secure, and smiled all through story time even though she arrived quiet and unwell.

qa.q: What did Ganga do to choose Gargi back?
qa.a: She saved Gargi the last orange slice and kept her surprise-card secret.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi to see Ganga smile?
qa.a: Gargi likely feels happy and trusted, seeing that her kindness made her friend feel better. 😊

grounding: A young girl's friend saves her a seat and calls her best friend, and she feels special and chooses her friend back.

passage: The school jeep bumped down the hill road. Dolma climbed in last, her cheeks cold. Every seat looked full. Then Vidya shifted her bag. "Dolma! I saved it for you. You're my best friend." Dolma squeezed in, warm at once. On the way home, Vidya whispered, "Don't tell. I'm making a paper flower for Amala Ma'am." Dolma nodded hard and kept her lips pressed shut. Next morning, Dolma climbed in first and kept her hand on the seat beside her. "For Vidya," she told the driver.

qa.q: What was Vidya making for Amala Ma'am?
qa.a: Vidya was making a paper flower for Amala Ma'am.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Vidya said she had saved the seat?
qa.a: She felt special and secure, warm at once after feeling cold and worried every seat was full.

qa.q: How does Dolma show that friendship goes both ways?
qa.a: She keeps Vidya's happy surprise secret and saves Vidya a seat the next morning.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when she finds her seat saved?
qa.a: Vidya probably feels chosen and happy, the same way Dolma felt the day before.

grounding: A young girl's friend saves her a seat and calls her best friend, and she learns to choose her friend back.

passage:
Note for Kashish's parents, from her class teacher.
Rekha was absent today with a cold. Kashish cried at the door and would not let go of her bag. At free play she sat alone in Rekha's usual spot and would not join anyone. I understand; they are very close. After snack I asked Kashish and two other girls to help me set up the pretend shop. Kashish was the shopkeeper. By home time she was laughing. Please keep inviting other children for short play dates too. Rekha will be glad to see her tomorrow. 🙂

qa.q: Why was Rekha absent?
qa.a: Rekha was absent with a cold.

qa.q: Why did Kashish sit alone in Rekha's spot?
qa.a: She felt sad and lost without her best friend, and felt unsafe playing with anyone else.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Kashish?
qa.a: The teacher gave her a job in a small group at the pretend shop, so she could connect with other children.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel tomorrow when she hears about the shop game?
qa.a: She may be glad to see Kashish again and maybe curious to join the new friends too.

grounding: A young girl cries and won't play with others when her best friend is absent, and a teacher helps her join a small group.

passage: At the anganwadi, Kunal kept looking at the door. Lalit wasn't coming; he had gone with his family to the sugarcane fields. Kunal sat by the window, his eyes wet, while the others played with the counting stones. "I want Lalit," he said. The didi who ran the anganwadi sat beside him. "You miss Lalit. He'll come back. Today, can you help Mohan and Radha build a stone tower?" Kunal shook his head. She held out one stone. He took it. Soon he was placing the top stone, and Radha clapped.

qa.q: Where had Lalit gone?
qa.a: He had gone with his family to the sugarcane fields.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling while he sat by the window?
qa.a: He felt sad and lonely, missing Lalit so much that he didn't want to play with anyone else.

qa.q: What small step helped Kunal join the others?
qa.a: The didi named his feeling and offered him one stone to help Mohan and Radha build a tower, a small group he could join.

qa.q: How might Radha see Kunal joining the tower?
qa.a: She may feel pleased to have a new helper, and clapping shows she welcomes him.

grounding: A young boy is sad and won't play when his best friend is away, and an adult helps him join a small group.

passage: It was raining, so the whole class was stuck indoors with only one skipping rope. Shreya and the new girl, Mehr, were turning it together. Irawati watched from the corner. Her chest felt burning hot. She marched up. "She's not allowed to play. Shreya is my friend." Mehr dropped the rope. Shreya looked upset. Irawati's tummy twisted. She took a breath. "I felt sad when you played without me." Shreya smiled. "You can turn too." Irawati picked up the rope end. "Mehr, you jump first."

qa.q: How many skipping ropes did the class have?
qa.a: They had only one skipping rope.

qa.q: What does Irawati's burning chest suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt jealous and afraid of losing Shreya to the new girl, and sad at being left out.

qa.q: What did Irawati do that fixed things?
qa.a: She said she felt sad and then invited Mehr to jump first, instead of shutting her out. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Mehr when Irawati says she's not allowed to play?
qa.a: It likely hurts Mehr and makes her feel unwelcome, which is why she drops the rope.

grounding: A young girl feels jealous when her friend plays with a new girl, tries to exclude her, then names her sadness and includes both.

passage: In the building lobby, Hemant was showing the new girl from the fourth floor his marble run. Alka stood by the lift, arms folded. Hemant was her friend. They always built the marble run together. A burning feeling rose up her chest. "She's not allowed," Alka said loudly. The girl, Jasleen, looked at her shoes. Hemant frowned. Alka's face felt hot. She looked at the marbles, then at Jasleen. "I felt sad because you didn't call me," she told Hemant. Then she knelt. "Jasleen, want the green marble?"

qa.q: What was Hemant showing the new girl?
qa.a: Hemant was showing her his marble run.

qa.q: How was Alka feeling as she stood by the lift?
qa.a: She felt jealous and left out, with a burning feeling in her chest, because Hemant was playing with someone new.

qa.q: What wise step did Alka take after saying "She's not allowed"?
qa.a: She told Hemant she felt sad and then invited Jasleen by offering her the green marble.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Alka's offer of the green marble?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and welcome after first feeling shut out.

grounding: A young girl feels jealous when her friend plays with a new girl, first excludes her, then names her sadness and invites her in.
